blocks.x: Okay, because when we were doing the recording at the Bulls Club, I know you and Chester's artists were talking about it. Oh yeah. And you know how you used to play there and I got really interested in it. And nobody seems to know anything about it.
Ain't that a shame? Well, yeah, people never, you know, actually I never went concerning this.
Yeah. Did you play there?

Yeah. When you were young? Yeah, sure. The other way, you're speaking up now? Yeah, I think so. Well, during those days, the bands used to mostly choose the nights. You see, they have dances and they had both yards on each side of the building, right and the left side.
There were two yards there?

Two yards, you see, facing, as we come in on that street, hominist street, facing the club. Well, to your right of the building, I see the other day when we was up there, they had some houses given to them. Well, they had a yard on that side. And then, you know, to the left of the building, like this would be the front of the building, like this, this would be the right, like I'm facing you, and this would be the left. Well, now, most likely to your right would be Kid Rene's band. They were supposed to have the best band. They were supposed to have the best band. Of course, you had, these three bands was really popular in them days. At that place was Kid Rene, Sam Morgan, and Chris Kelly, you see, during them days. Now, about every Tuesday night, you'll have two groups playing in there, and they're all just being packed with people. And as long as I was going up there like that, sometimes we'd play with different mixed groups in there. Sometimes I'd play in there with a fellow by the name of Bud Russel on bass violin, he played the bass violin. A fellow by the name of Arthur William Clarinet. And a man by the name of Leo Sanjay playing banjo. And, let me see, he was playing the trombone. Sometime he was on trombone. There was, I can't think of that guy's name in the present. I know it wasn't Rob. It was a guy from Uptown. Oh, boy, that's something. Let me see, I really can't think of his name. A man from Uptown? Yeah, he was, I know, it was all about the name. Henry? No, it was, he's dead and gone. Is that name, we call it Joe Avery. Oh, Joe Avery. Joe Avery. Joe Avery, yeah.
I've heard of him.
Yeah, Joe Avery.
This was on the weekends?

Yeah, well, sometimes we played like on weekends, like, mostly Tuesday nights, the weekends, but most of the time they'd run on that. Any other things be given, they'd be special occasions. But the dancers on Tuesday was especially affairs like that, you see, just like the Santa Senders. Yeah. Well, that club used to run their own dances and the high outside people could, you know, always rent the hall for different occasions. Yeah. Excuse me.
Let me stop and check it and see. Yeah. Okay. Well, you mean, like, where was the bar? Did they have that bar there?
The bar be mostly on inside of the hall. Inside the hall. Inside the hall.
You mean, like that bar we went in, you know, to get drinks the other day, was that there then?

No, I can't remember, Jane, of that same place. No, I don't believe that section was there, no, because sometimes they may put, like, little private tables on our side, you know, put like tablecloths or something on it, or a piece of white cloth in front of it. But the place would be so jam-packed during them nights, you see, on both yards would be crowded. And I would say like the other night, the fifth day when we was making a recording, the voices say you could hear when you're playing like Kelly's Love, that old slow blues, that little slow drag, like, you know, that's where the word drag comes from. You could hear the heels of the people, this smooth down on the ground. Really? On the outside? On the outside. Oh wow. Some people, like they go in dreamland, the bands be playing it so slow, you know. And the best group for me could play that number was Chris Kelly.
And where did he play? Inside the hall or in the yard? In the yard.
In the yard. In the yard. In the yard. All the bands played in the yard.
You mean they would have three bands playing?
No, two bands. Two bands. Yeah, one on each side. One on the right side of the building, one on the left side.
But who would play inside?
No bands at all, unless you go to the rain or something, or maybe over cold weather. Oh I see. Most of them affairs was outside, Tuesday, Tuesday night.
Well when did they use the inside?
Well I guess on different occasions, but every time I used to attend the place, it'd be mostly used to be on the arts in the yards.
Well I wonder what they used the inside for, they must use it for a dance hall.
Well they used it for different years, sure, they used it for the dance hall, and of course it was remodeled like it is now, you know, that's not true.
Well did they, like now they've got it all modeled, you know, they put the pine walls and everything, did it used to have windows?
Oh yeah, sure, they had windows, that's right. On both sides?
Both sides, yeah.

They had windows, but I'm still puzzled, like you asked me about them houses, because that's right to your right, otherwise where that little small lounge is at, that was part of the yard. Oh I see. Yeah, to the right side of the building, you see the building. So that lounge is new then.
That's had to be something new.

The Elks must have built that house. Yeah, well the Elks took the bulls over. Now speaking about that, because you see the Elks, they first, when I joined the Elks, it was on a street called, on Drysdale, Melpomene, used to be the old Mason Hall. Yeah, I believe I was sworn in the Elks in 1935, during the WPA, URA band time, that's when I was a man in Elk, and of course I stood in a good while and just dropped right on out like that. But during them areas and that, I'll bring it back to the bulls' time. Now, speaking about the night parades, now where two places I feel they could get the bulls from, they used in their night parades to be in their truck, they had one large bull, they had to get two places, they could be called the Crescent City Slaughterhouse, that's way down in the night ward, and they'll have a live hour bull, and they'll have, each side of his home they'll have a rope tied around it, to the wing of the truck, I mean the sides of the truck, and he'd come along in the middle of the parade when they, they're making, en route like that. At night? That's right, at night, and they had what you call these little flambeau lights, you know, and all the men have that, and they have their fun like that. And I was there at that time living on the street they called Seminard between Vera and Robison.
Yeah, the big wide street?

The big wide street, yeah. They hadn't paved it then, during them days it used to be like these bricks-like, something just like North Peter Street is. You see, that's what you call the Tor blocks. But during them Seminard Avenue had them little bricks. Well, the parade would come down, far as Claiborne, I imagine they'd go to the Frenchman Street, make a ton, and come up Claiborne, and where'd they go from there, I wouldn't know. But that's how we all would call it the circle during them days, you see, because that you had the old North Claiborne Street car used to run through there, and we had, in the middle of the neutral ground they had a paving. People used to walk through there at night, the summer nights, meet girls and their friends, and they'd by just walk up and down. Some people in the evening time, cheering, skating. Yeah, like a little park. Yeah, but it used to run all together from Canal and Claiborne, clean on down to Elision Field Avenue, that neutral ground did, and the street calls on each side, in the neutral ground running, and they didn't have much traffic like you got now, you see. And then as far as when you leave Claiborne and Canal, it'd run a piece, and then we had, near Tulane there we had the Claiborne Market there, it used to block you off.
Is that near where the Circle Market is now?
Yeah, where the Circle was at now, that used to be nothing but houses there.
Oh really?
Yeah, you see the market used, I mean the Seminar Market was right there, but it wasn't that kind of building, it was built like on the old side, something like the French Market.
Oh I see, so the Circle Market is pretty near.

Yeah, well the Circle was a grocery store, but it first started to crawl down. The first Seminar Market, I can remember, it wasn't named, it was called, you had the butcher stands, and you had the vegetable stand to the front part of the building, and across the street from there where you see a brick building, that used to be Maggie Gagne's hardware store. You see that brick, and when that caught a fire, years back, I forgot this was year that happened, when that caught, and during that same time the fire they had like a rain, a rain flood. It flood the street, the wall almost up to the side steps on the sidewalk. Well Maggie Gagne had the hardware store there for years and years, and next to the Seminar Market used to be the alley, and next to the alley had a feed store there, you see, and all those new buildings come up there, and then come two little single white houses, you see, and some of the houses still stands there, outside of the alley is gone, because it's the door. Then next to the Seminar Market too, during them days, they had like a two-story building, it was down there called Steinmann, the Jewish guy had a dry goods store, like a notion store there, called Steinmann's, you see, and then when you go between the market and Steinmann's a notion store, you had the alley, it was run by these people here called, they used to run the old lottery shops, the Andre Dominguez. The Dominguez? Yeah, Andre Dominguez. I've never heard of that. Yeah, they look like Spanish type people, Andre Dominguez. Let me see, wait now. Yeah, you know that stuff, but I think it was Andre Dominguez. Well they lived there for years and years on the street called North Romant between Seminar and New Orleans Street, yeah. They stood there for, now that same house where they was living at, they took that house and they made it like a apartment. Yeah, they made it that distance to that, on North Romant Street. But the alley, doing it, was in full blowing during them days, and such bands like Moorish Duran, and playing the trumpet, a fellow by the name, George, he's still living, do a drummer by the name of, I said, Jen, you've got to run that over here, because I can't think of them guys' names. Yeah, and I don't know him, so I can't, but I can't help you. Yeah, I know you don't know him, but I'm trying to play the drum then. Then we had Dodon on banjo, Moorish Duran trumpet, and this boy by the name of George Sutton playing the drum. He was playing, sometimes this kind of little four or five piece band, you'd do an alley there.
And, yeah, yeah, and you would play just around in this little section?

Right in the alley, you see they had a bar in like a little nightclub, you could call it, right in the back. Like the bar, you come into the alley between the market and the Steinmetz and Ocean's store, and as you come in through that alley like that, you come into, it'd be like a regular bar, you know? I see, yeah. Of course, that would control the people off now by having that seminar circles, and the circle people, they come in there later years after. But I'm bringing it back to a time when you had, the meat wouldn't be in these refrigerators like these people, they'd be on the butcher stands, they'd come there early in the morning, and they'd hang up upon like on these hooks. The stand view, you know, open stands, you see? Yeah. And you could then, when the market closed between 12-1 and the daytime, where they'd put their meats in these big old, old-time ice boxes on the outside. Oh, I see. So, yeah. And the Iceman, you had no fridges there, the Iceman used to pack the, you know, the packed ice on the meat. And every early Sunday mornings like that, where the markets would be open, you know, you could see that all over the door. The first year had wagons, horse drawings with two horses or two mules, bringing the meat from the Christian City Slaughter Company, or either the Northern Butcher Abattoir, bringing the meat to these different butcher stands, and then they'd turn around and put it on the stand, it's like that, even before the bitches, you know, get there. And when the butchers come, maybe 5 o'clock in the morning, well, they start cutting meat like they want to hang it up on them hooks. And then, of course, during them times, you had no border help to say that the meat could just be spoiled, you understand? And that's how the meat was sold. And then mostly, then you had the live chickens, chickens being cages. You could buy a live chicken, they could, you know, kill it right there for you, or you would take it home yourself, you know, and bring it in your market basket.
That's what, yeah, everybody would come every morning and do their shopping.

That's right. Yeah, do their shopping. They liked the day people could buy so much meat and all, half a side of a beef, or a cow like that, and stir it away. Freeze it all over there. Freeze it all over there for months and months, you know. That's like, people.
Sounds like a, it sounds like a very, you know, pleasant way to live, very uncomplicated.

Yeah, it was, people lived healthy. I mean, during the days, we didn't have freezer days, but they sure bought the meat like that, and they had it live on, you know, on the meat stands. And then, it used to do you good to see the, when they closed during the daytime, they used to take like these, these long, we call them cane knives, you know, and scrape, you know, like the meat stains off the, off the, off the meat stand, you see. They used to scrape that down.

That's fascinating. And the, well, you, you've always lived downtown. All my life, yeah. And then the Bulls Club would parade downtown. Come down Claiborne Street. All the way down? All the way down Claiborne.

All the way down Claiborne. I imagine Forest Frenchman Street, yeah. Good street. Then they'd come on the downtown side, which would be the riverside, that's how we call it them days. Yeah. And then get on the lakeside and come up. And like I say, where they started, I can't remember, where the parade force began. Then, essentially, speaking about the Bulls, we had another club, it was called the Hop Goblins. Now what were they? That was most consistent of women folks too, of night parades. Sometimes they had carriages, horse-drawn carriages, and that was beautiful too. They had the flambeau lights. Were they all in costumes?
Different costumes, right.
Were they from Uptown, the Hop Goblins? I think Hop Goblins from Uptown, that's right.
And they were, were they like the ladies auxiliary of the Bulls Club, or were they completely separate?
Well, I think they were separate from the Bulls, the Hop Goblins. It was a different organization.
Yeah, because like, you know, you have the Elks and then the ladies auxiliary and the Zulus and the Luz.
That's right, yeah, ladies auxiliary. I just wonder if they had any connection with them.
Well, they could be a branch.

There's something like, speaking like in the Catwood religion, you see, they take the nice Peter Claibor, the line of the college. Well, the men's college, they had the chartered first, Knights of Peter Claibor, and then the women's, they fall, they call the ladies auxiliary, Knights of Peter Claibor. Yeah, that's what I was thinking about.
Of course, the Bulls Club isn't like the Knights of Peter Claibor.

Oh, no, no, no, that's mostly a secret organization. The Bulls Club is nothing but a pleasure organization. It's like the Hop Goblins. And then we had the Sanders Centers, that was all pleasure clubs. Were you in there? I was a member of the Sanders Centers. Really? I didn't know that. Yeah, I was a member of the Sanders Centers for years and years. And we had this, when they was on Dumaine Street, and there was another of them down. The Lions, they was located on Dumaine right where Lopez got the Undertaker part. The same house still stands there, yeah. The Lions Club? The Lions, yeah, that was another club.
I've never heard of that. Was it a pleasure club?
Not a pleasure club, just like the Sims like the Bulls. They prayed, but none of them was prayed like the Bulls. The Sanders Centers never had no large prayers like the Bulls Club.
They just had the clubhouse and the meetings. Right.

They'd have a meeting right there, rent out their hall to a different organization or give their own dances like that. Now their favorite band during them days used to be Sam Morgan Band at the Sanchez Centers. Just like the Creole people down my way, if you hire any other band, they had better bands than Sam, but everybody could see Sam Morgan Band in my section, you see.
Who played Dronsfield Morgan's band most of the time?
Alfred Williams.
Alfred Williams, yeah.

I'll give you the band over there, the band I'm speaking about during them days was I line them up like how we used to line them up. First come the drum in a row, then come the trombone, Yank on trombone, Alfred Williams on drums, Yank on trombone, Sam Morgan on trumpet, then come Zeb clarinet, then come Johnny Dave banjo, and then come to beat the bass violin. They didn't use pianists? No, no pianists. Now and then they use a piano. They use it on the record. Yeah, they use piano to make records though, but most of the bands in them days consist of six pieces. You have a bass on this end, drum on that end, and then all the horns, bass, violon, banjo, clarinet, trumpet, cornet, no trumpet, cornet, the trombone, and drum. That's how we line them up.
Oh yeah, they're sitting on the long row. Long row, that's right, yeah.
That's how they line up in them days. And the bands would be off the floor. You had like a little small balcony, like a little bandstand.
They never sit in two rows like they do, no?

No, no, no. They're in the back and the front. No, no, no, no. Right across the row, like this. Give me this pencil, I'll show you. Yeah. See, they go right down the line, just like this. This be a drum. This is right in the row. Drum, trombone, cornet, clarinet, banjo, and bass. You see, it's six bands. I see.
You can picture that. They never have the bands sit like that anymore, no? No, they don't do that, no. But they don't build the bandstand like that.
On the old-time bands, there's not room for a piano.

Yeah, you see, the old-time bandstand, of course, the Carparelli's Hall is the, I don't know, they didn't knock that down. Yeah, the Carparelli's Hall, that's to be on Liberty Street. That used to be another famous hall, but now the Sandus Cinders had a piano on their bandstand. You see, now you can line up a band, when the Sandus Cinders, the piano beat mostly to the back wall, then you put your drummer there, and you put your banjo on that side. Most likely banjo player had to be almost like on the left side of the piano player, you see. And then your horns would be in the front. So when the band went to eight pieces, well that's where a fellow by the name of Oriel Fusche, he left our band, the Young Tuxedo, and went into the Sam Morgan band, which he don't blame me, because they had more work. Our band, this was coming up, taking Carparelli after the original Tuxedo band. You see, that's where around 19, between 24 and 25, 27, all like that.
I want to ask you something more about the Morgan band. How long did Gaynor play with that band?
Well, George Gaynor played mostly in the replacing Johnny Dave. See, Johnny Dave.
Later years, you mean? Later years, right.

See, Johnny Dave was a number one plaster, and when the band used to go over like, most of the places used to be like Biloxi, Mobile, Bay St. Louis, not too much Gulfport, Biloxi, Mississippi, Bay St. Louis, and Mobile, Alabama. At that time the band used to travel.
That's where they used to go on.
Right, yeah. When the band go on the trips like that, it was most likely. George Gino used to replace Johnny Dave.
Well, Dave didn't want to go out of town.

Well, Johnny Dave by working and playing his band, George, he's plaster working on me playing this, doing his plaster work. Yeah. But as long as the band, so George Gino, one time before, he's dead and gone, and this gave me the report like he explained it to me. He told Sam if he's going to always go with the band when they're going out of town, and the band being the city here making the big hit, let the public see him, he don't want to go no more with him. So that's why they decided to keep George Gino all together.
So he became a steady member.
A steady member with the band.
And when did Henry Ross come into picture? He claims that he played with Morgan Band too. Was that in the later years too? Well I don't know.
It might have been the later years, but I knew young Morgan had a band. You see now, young Morgan Band had Jim on trombone, his nephew Jim Little on bass, Rudolph John Drum, and Andrew Morgan.
This must have been the band that Henry Ross played with. Yes, they might have played with that group, you see.
But the reason with Sam Morgan, man, I can't pitch him.
I can't pitch him. I pitch him Henry and Russ playing with them. When did that young band start out? Was that in the late 20s or something?

Oh, yeah, during the 20s, that was all in their range. All them bands were separate to themselves. The young Morgan Band was to itself, Sam he was to himself. I see. You see them guys there was two brothers.
I think Henry Russ must have come into that later. You know, later.
You see now he had a brother by the name of Albert Morgan, I think he was the best musician of all them guys.
The bass player.

Bass player, yeah. He played the bass horn and the bass violin, and they always dressed doodified. And he used to hang on it mostly by the old Astoria on South Ramports. He used to be running by these people here, the Braden family.
Did he play with any of the Morgan Band too? Who, me?
The L. Albert. Well, I don't know, not being no regular member, no.
I don't remember.
He was younger than the- He was younger, yeah, Albert Morgan, he was much younger, and all the family, yeah. Yeah. But Andrew Morgan, he played with his Young Morgan Band.
Uh-huh. That's the band that's recorded there. Oh, yeah. The Young Morgan Band, yeah.
That's with Andrew Morgan and Jim.
So the old, the old original Sam Morgan Band was back, was that before World War I? Or after World War I?

Oh, no, I would have been in the- Well, I don't remember, Jenny, from after World War I. It was- Yeah. I was much younger then, because that's happened around then. Yeah. Yeah. The World War, just about nine months. But Young Morgan, I mean Andrew, my time of seeing the bands during them, they was around 90, 90, 90, 20. Yeah, after the war. Right. That was way before the Young Morgan Band started out, do you think? Oh, yeah, Sam had this band before Young Morgan Band. Oh, yeah, yeah.
Naturally, yeah. And that, yeah. Yeah. And I think the band that recorded, what's the United 27 or something?
Something.
It was a late 20. Yeah, that must have been what you called a Young Morgan Band. Yeah, well- At Jim and Earl Fusier and those people.
Yeah, well that's when Earl Fusier, you speak about the year in 27 when I made my voice recording.
Right, around the same time as the cell phone.

Yeah, we made that by the Columbia people on Canal Street. Mm-hmm. And during that week, that's when everybody laughs about John, they use the word, but Sandball got the best go year. Yeah. Yeah, that's the times you used, the best go year. Well, that's Johnny Day played on that record. Right, right. That's right.
What band was that?

That was the Young Morgan Band. Well, they called it Sam Morgan Band. Sam Morgan Band. Sam Morgan Band. But, say, Sammy got the best go year. You know, Johnny Day, I picked him right now, standing on Seminole in Claiborne waiting to catch the North Claiborne called the Ride Up Canal Street. Yeah. Well, that same year you're speaking about was John Morrell had got several fellas out there in the tuxedo band to make that record. I see. And he had wanted, Chani Bebe was the drummer, you see, but he was a crack drummer. But they wanted me to play on the con and they figured Chani might get high or something and blow him up. Not for better playing, but this figure that, this like in 1930 when I went over to Biloxo with Tuxedo Band, they played at a seasoned job at the Buena Vista Hotel. And see they had what they called stop time. And then for the Gitter Man, so I was playing with the Piran Band during them days, and they asked me to play that's a seasoned job. It starts in, it ends up on a Labor Day, but it starts in I think in the middle part of July. It's supposed to be ten weeks or something like that. Yeah. Well we used to play from, how that was, from eleven to twelve in the day called Breakfast Dance. It's still running? Yeah. And then we played from five to six, and then we'd come back and go play from nine to twelve. Monday's True Sadness, and you had the Mississippi Blue Law, we'd come home on a Sunday with those who want to come home. That was where I bring it back in 1930 now. That's when I played that season with the Tuxedo Band. I'll give you the members of that band. Yeah, yeah. Well that band at that time consisted of, first had Bill Matthew on trombone, and Papa Celeste on cornet, and Rick High Lexie on cornet, two cornets. And the sax session consisted of a boy by the name of Sun Johnson, he's on this picture here now, he was good, and we had Joe Ruzon, he's out in L.A. right now on sax, another good man, and we had this boy, Edmund Hall, that's the other one, Clarence Hall on tenor sax.
So Paul Barch wasn't doing that band anymore then? Who? Paul Barch was gone. Oh no, no. He was up in New York that time.

Paul Barch wouldn't play in the band that time, got to play in 1930. And then during that time when Joe Ruzon got hoisted, had like a B or something, he kind of hoisted his mouth, so we replaced him with this fellow Caesar Thornton. Yeah, yeah. Yeah, he's from St. Louis, and he came down here on the boat. Not too much with sax, but he was a good arranger. They had him play with the band, he finished it there, and then he started arranging for the band while he was on the seasoned job. And then come down, and Jeanette was, I mean, Mercedes Gorman was playing the piano in Jeanette Sullivan's place, because he was expecting a first child.
I see.

You see, that's Marvin Kimmel's wife. Right. Jeanette's, well we called her Sullivan, but I don't think she, yeah she married to Kimmel then, that's right. So I used to bring money for him, for Kimmel to help people, that girl came from, from, uh, uh, Patschristian, Mississippi. Mm-hmm. And every Sunday, Kimmel had a Buick Roast call, and I had a force on the Dodge call, well I used to drive home every Sunday, and go back on a Monday morning, well I used to ride Caesar, that's all the sax section, and sometimes Rick, he's still over the lake too, because he's from the Bay St. Louis, you see. Yeah. And that's his little brother playing the drum right now by the Mason Boybin.
Right.

Yeah. And Lester. Yeah, Little Lester, and them boys was all small in there. Yeah, that was the group. I was on the drum, yeah. Mm-hmm. That was the band. So Merced Deez was playing in Jeanette Sullivan's place. I see. Yeah, with that band, dude. That was 1930.
And how long did you stay with that band?

Well I just played the job with him, I went back to my band. I see, yes. I stood in Pierron's band until he broke up the old band in 1932, then he took over a band they called the Sonny South. Uh-huh.
That was another good outfit.

He quit the old band, Pierron did, and that's up, that's called Peter Bocard, and then they made up another group they called the Creole Serenades. Mm-hmm. You see, that's the picture you've got now. Oh yeah. That's the Creole Serenades. Henry Martin on drum, Dwight Newman on piano, Andrew Bocard, Charlie Bocard, and Peter Bocard.
Oh, let me ask you about another band that we don't have much information on. Do you remember anything about the Nola band? Oh yeah, Peter Bocard, yeah. Who was in that band? Who was in that band?
Yeah, Peter Bocard, yeah.
Who else was in that band that you remember?
You see, I might, right now, I know Henry Ross played with the band. Yeah, now you're coming the right way. Yeah. You're coming here, that's Peter Bocard.
We haven't told Peter Bocard, if we're going to go see him right way.
Yeah, he's Daniel Ralphs on Seminoid Street, poor fella, he's the number one wheel writer. He was the leader of that band.
Oh sure, oh, one of them good ones.
You remember who played clarinet in that band?
No, I'm trying to think.

No, no, it's the Monsieur. That's one band, I know them guys, but I can't at present just think of them guys' names. But I can tell you, one band he had was a good one, was Willigan's, a drummer. Who's that? Willigan's. Willigan's?
What is his first name?
Yeah, I don't know Willigan's first name, but he was a crack drummer. I can tell you about him, yeah.
I see.
Willigan's, he's a little guy, I like the auger plenty, he was a good drummer though, yeah. He was a little small fella, something like Chani, whatever they have before us.
Was that a six piece band?
It's all six piece band, yeah. Peter Locard, no, I can't think of all them men that present who play with the noted band, jazz band.
They changed name on that band, though. They called it Henry Russell, they called it Silvertone band one time. Yeah, possibly, yeah.

You see, well how them fellas in them days do them things is, just like what caused me to get into the Piran band was Walter Pichon came at the old place they called the Pelican, it was run by the Astoria. The Pelican was located on Grabin' Ramp, which you got a parking lot in there. That's another place used to run, much famous as the Bull, because some nights they'd have four bands that would play up there.
Oh wow.

And the Pack House that was located on the court had the restaurant and ball and pool table downstairs. They called it, they was run by this fella by the name of Faubacher. And this fella, Bebe, William Ridgely's brother, he was the manager of the place. I think I don't know, remember his name? His first name? Yeah, his first name was Bebe Ridgely, his first name, he was a big tall, brown skin, heavy built man. But he was the manager of that place there, I can't think of his first name.
